plan: [No prior rounds to learn from. With 5 bidders and third-price payment, the third-order statistic of five uniform draws has mean ~24.5, so bidding my true value is a safe, near-optimal strategy: it wins when the third-highest is below my value and avoids overbidding risk that could produce negative payoff. I will bid my private value to maximize expected surplus while keeping downside limited.]

[Assume opponents bid their values (uniform 0–49). If I bid b and win, the expected payment is the second-highest of four opponents = 0.6b, and win probability=(b/49)^4. Maximizing expected surplus (35−0.6b)*(b/49)^4 yields optimal b≈140/3≈46.67. This increases my win chance while keeping expected payment below my value. Use 0.1 granularity, so bid 46.7. If opponents shade differently, this aggressive bid still raises long-run profit by capturing high-value wins.]

[Value = $6, no prior history. Assuming other bidders bid their values, if I win by bidding b I pay the second-highest among the other four with expected payment 0.6b and win probability (b/49)^4. Expected profit ≈ (b/49)^4*(6−0.6b). Maximizing this on [0,10] gives interior optimum at b=8. Bid $8 to balance higher win probability against overpayment risk.]

[With 5 bidders and a third-price rule, overbidding slightly above my value increases win probability while the price paid (the third-highest) stays relatively low. For uniform values, the symmetric optimal bid is about (n-1)/(n-2)*v = 4/3 * 10 ≈ 13.33. That maximizes expected profit against likely opponent behavior while respecting independent redraws. I’ll bid $13.3.]

[I assume opponents bid their true values (uniform 0–49). If I bid b, win probability = (b/49)^4 and conditional on winning the expected payment is the 2nd-highest of 4 opponents = 0.6b, so expected payoff ∝ b^4(19−0.6b). Maximizing gives b = 76/3 ≈ 25.33. This produces positive expected surplus when I win. With $0.1 increments I will bid 25.3 to approximate the optimum and maximize long-run expected profit under these assumptions.]
